newsitem.title: USA: Japanese rate hike talk pressures dollar.
newsitem.headline: Japanese rate hike talk pressures dollar.

text.p: NEW YORK, Oct 7 - The dollar fell against the Japanese yen Monday after two senior Japanese politicians suggested interest rates in Japan might soon head higher.
The Bank of Japan has kept its official discount rate at a record low of 0.5 percent since September 1995 to stimulate economic growth.

Shizuka Kamei, head of the Liberal Democratic Party press office, was quoted in news reports as saying on Monday that a rise in Japan's official discount rate will probably be considered after general elections. The Liberal Democratic Party is the largest member of a three-party ruling coalition in Japan. Elections are scheduled for Oct. 20.
Separately, Ichiro Ozawa, head of the main opposition New Frontier Party or Shinshinto, also said on Monday that Japan's interest rate levels must be corrected.
The Bank of Japan declined to comment on the rate talk.
Higher interest rates would help the Japanese currency by making yen-denominated deposits more attractive to foreign investors.
The remarks fuelled demand for yen in Asia, which carried over when trade got underway in Europe and New York.
"They're buying yen and selling everything that's been bought the last couple of weeks," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer & Co.

The dollar slid as low as 111.05 yen in New York but later trimmed its losses. In late New York trading, the dollar fetched 111.19 yen and 1.5312 German marks, down from 111.79 yen and 1.5323 marks late Friday.

Although the politicians' comments jolted a foreign exchange market sensitive to signs that rates in Japan will climb, some analysts dismissed the comments as a ploy to please Japanese savers dissatisfied with the country's rock bottom interest rates.

"I view it mainly as political posturing ahead of the election," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International. "I don't think either party is serious about raising rates without economic justification for it."
Growing optimism that the European Union will successfully launch a common currency as planned in January 1999 continued to pressure the mark relative to some other European currencies.
The mark's status as a safe-haven currency is diminished by a belief that the effort to establish a single currency or Euro will succeed.
The European Union's monetary committee meets on Tuesday to move foreward on key factors including a budget stability pact for countries joining the single currency.

"I think that there's no question the overall consensus of the market is that EMU (European Monetary Union) will go ahead and will go ahead on schedule," said William Marr, manager of foreign exchange at Credit Commerciale de France. "It's just a question now of a little bit of jockeying in terms of what the market consensus is on whose going to be the first members."
The Italian lira, Spanish peseta and French franc strengthened against the German currency.
Expectation that Italy will soon re-enter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) also bolstered the lira.

The Italian currency crashed out of the ERM during a currency crisis in September 1992. Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi requested last week that talks start quickly on the level at which the lira might re-enter the system.
"The market is reluctant to sell off lira with the possibility the French and Germans will insist on lira appreciation before ERM entry," McCarthy said.

The lira lost up to 40 percent of its value after its ERM ejection, boosting Italian export competitiveness. Since 1995, the lira has rebounded about 20 percent and cost around 990 per mark in late Monday.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.2545 Swiss francs from 1.2579 Swiss francs late Tuesday. The British pound slid to $1.5639 from $1.5649. The dollar dipped to Canadian $1.3532 from C$1.3544.
